اجتماع سابق بين محمد المنفي رئيس المجلس الرئاسي الليبي وحسين العايب في طرابلس (مكتب المنفي)
احتدم النزاع مجدداً على قيادة جهاز الاستخبارات الليبية، بعد صدور حكم قضائي جديد بوقف تنفيذ قرار المجلس الرئاسي الذي أعفى حسين العايب من رئاسة الجهاز، وكلف عبد المجيد مليقطة خلفاً له.
وقضت محكمة استئناف الزاوية، دائرة القضاء الإداري، مساء الأحد، في الشق المستعجل من الطعن الإداري رقم «173» لسنة 2026، بوقف تنفيذ قرارات المجلس الرئاسي المتعلقة بإعفاء العايب وتكليف مليقطة برئاسة الجهاز وتعيين نائب له.
ويشكّل الحكم أحدث حلقة في نزاع قضائي وسياسي مستمر، ويعيد الجدل بشأن الجهة التي تملك صلاحية تغيير قيادة جهاز الاستخبارات، أحد أبرز الأجهزة السيادية والأمنية في ليبيا.
وقبل صدور هذا الحكم، وفي تطور يعكس احتدام الصراع حول تمثيل الجهاز، أصدر الجهاز مؤخراً تعميماً حذر فيه من التعامل مع العايب، أو أي جهة تتصرف باسمه، مؤكداً أن صفته رئيساً للجهاز انتهت منذ 29 يونيو (حزيران)، وأن مليقطة هو المخوّل بتمثيل الجهاز والتصرف باسمه.
وبينما يستند العايب إلى الطعن والأحكام القضائية التي أوقفت تنفيذ قرارات إعفائه، واصل مليقطة تحركاته بصفته رئيساً للجهاز، حيث التقى في أذربيجان رئيس جهاز الاستخبارات العامة المصري اللواء حسن رشاد الذي هنّأه بتوليه مهامه، وأكد دعم مصر لتعزيز التعاون والتنسيق بين الجهازين.
وبحث الجانبان -حسب جهاز الاستخبارات الليبية- توسيع التعاون وتبادل المعلومات في مكافحة الإرهاب والجريمة المنظمة والهجرة غير النظامية والتهريب وتأمين الحدود، إلى جانب التطورات الإقليمية، مؤكدين أهمية التنسيق الأمني بين ليبيا ومصر لدعم أمن واستقرار البلدين وشمال أفريقيا.
كما اجتمع مليقطة مع رئيس جهاز أمن الدولة الأذربيجاني علي ناغييف الذي هنّأه بتولي مهامه الجديدة وبمنصب رئيس لجنة أجهزة الأمن والمخابرات الأفريقية.
كما التقى مليقطة رئيس الاستخبارات السوداني أحمد إبراهيم، وبحث معه -حسب الاستخبارات الليبية- تطورات الأوضاع في السودان وانعكاساتها على الأمن الإقليمي.
وكان مليقطة قد أعلن اعتماده رئيساً للجنة أجهزة الأمن والمخابرات الأفريقية (سيسا)، التي تضم أجهزة الأمن والاستخبارات في 53 دولة أفريقية، وتتولى تعزيز التعاون والتنسيق الأمني والاستخباراتي بين دول القارة.
وجاء اعتماد مليقطة -وفقاً لجهاز الاستخبارات- بصفته «الرئيس الشرعي للجهاز»، فيما تتخذ اللجنة من العاصمة الإثيوبية أديس أبابا مقراً لأمانتها.
وكان المجلس الرئاسي، برئاسة محمد المنفي، قد أصدر في يونيو الماضي قراراً بإعفاء العايب وتكليف مليقطة، وهو ما أثار خلافاً داخل المجلس نفسه، بعدما أعلن عضو المجلس موسى الكوني رفضه تغيير قيادة الجهاز.
ولجأ العايب إلى القضاء للطعن في القرارات، في حين تمسكت السلطات الداعمة لمليقطة بكون قرارات المجلس الرئاسي نافذة.
ويأتي حكم محكمة استئناف الزاوية بعد أحكام وأوامر قضائية أخرى تناولت القرارات نفسها، ما أدى إلى تعقيد الوضع القانوني حول قيادة الجهاز، لكنه لا يعني حسم أصل النزاع الموضوعي، وإنما يضيف عقبة قضائية جديدة أمام استمرار تنفيذ قرارات المجلس الرئاسي.
وبينما يواصل العايب الدفاع عن «شرعيته» عبر المسار القضائي، يسعى مليقطة إلى تثبيت صفته من خلال ممارسة مهامه والظهور في اتصالات رسمية خارج ليبيا.
ويأتي الحكم القضائي الأخير ضمن سلسلة أوامر وأحكام قضائية سابقة صادرة عن محاكم ليبية مختلفة، من بينها محكمة استئناف بنغازي في أغسطس (آب) الماضي التي أوقفت تنفيذ القرارات نفسها إلى حين الفصل في الطعون.
وفجرت قرارات المنفي، المستندة إلى الإعلان الدستوري والاتفاق السياسي ومخرجات «ملتقى الحوار السياسي»، وشملت إعفاء العايب وتكليف مليقطة وتعيين عبد الشفيع حسين نائباً؛ انقساماً فورياً داخل المجلس الرئاسي نفسه.
ورغم الجدل، تولى مليقطة فعلياً إدارة بعض المقرات في طرابلس، والتقى رئيس حكومة الوحدة المؤقتة عبد الحميد الدبيبة في العاصمة طرابلس.

title: 'El Poder de las Personas', el documental que narra la lucha de líderes con discapacidad intelectual
content:
'El Poder de las Personas', el documental que narra la lucha de líderes con discapacidad intelectual por lograr la ciudadanía plena
Basado en hechos observados y verificados directamente por nuestros periodistas o por fuentes informadas.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
Creado por Plena Inclusión España, esta pieza recoge testimonios de activistas con discapacidad intelectual que reivindican su derecho a decidir sobre sus propias vidas.
Plena inclusión España presenta en estos días el video-documental ‘El Poder de las Personas’, una producción audiovisual que da voz a personas con discapacidad intelectual y del desarrollo que, desde diferentes lugares de España, llevan años peleando por una reivindicación histórica: ser reconocidas como ciudadanas y ciudadanos de pleno derecho, con presencia, voz y voto en los espacios públicos de decisión dónde aportar su punto de vista e influir en la sociedad.
A través de relatos en primera persona, el documental muestra la historia reciente del papel ejercido por líderes con discapacidad intelectual y del desarrollo, y de las asociaciones en las que participan. Su lucha ha influido de forma decisiva en los avances logrados respecto al acceso a derechos básicos para más de 400.000 personas con discapacidad intelectual y del desarrollo que residen en nuestros barrios y pueblos. No obstante, los testimonios recogidos señalan que todavía existen importantes obstáculos para estas personas en el acceso igualitario a derechos y oportunidades en igualdad de condiciones.
La participación en foros públicos, la autorrepresentación y el liderazgo son aspectos destacados por ‘El Poder de las Personas’ de quienes han visto limitada su presencia en los espacios de decisión hasta hace bien poco.
Una de las protagonistas destacadas en el video-documental es Ana Martínez, funcionaria, artista y activista de los derechos de las personas con discapacidad intelectual, que además representa a España en la Plataforma Europea de Autorrepresentantes (EPSA). La pieza también recoge la experiencia de ‘Los que No se Rinden’, la primera asociación española integrada exclusivamente por personas con discapacidad intelectual y del desarrollo para defender sus derechos y promover su participación social y política.
La producción incluye además testimonios de líderes como Horacio Peláez, activista y miembro de la Plataforma Estatal de Representantes; Maribel Cáceres, vicepresidenta de Plena inclusión España. También se escuchan las voces de representantes institucionales y sociales como Pablo Bustinduy, ministro de Derechos Sociales, Consumo y Agenda 2030; Jesús Martín, director general de Derechos de las Personas con Discapacidad; o de Enrique Galván, director de Plena inclusión España.
Uno de los ejes centrales del documental es el movimiento de autorrepresentación impulsado por personas con discapacidad intelectual y del desarrollo. El vídeo repasa también algunos de los hitos que han marcado esta lucha colectiva. Relata la relevancia de de la reforma de la Ley Electoral de 2018, que permitió recuperar el derecho al voto a más de 100.000 personas, o la creación en 2021 de la Plataforma Estatal de Representantes de Personas con Discapacidad Intelectual y del Desarrollo, una tribuna desde la que estas personas trasladan sus demandas a instituciones públicos o al movimiento asociativo, y que les permite participar en el debate público.
‘El Poder de las Personas’ muestra cómo la participación no es solo un derecho, sino también una herramienta imprescindible para combatir la invisibilización, los prejuicios y la infantilización que todavía afectan a muchas personas con discapacidad intelectual.
La película también pone en valor el papel de las familias, de las organizaciones sociales y de las redes de apoyo que han acompañado durante décadas la defensa de los derechos de este colectivo, contribuyendo a avances legislativos y sociales que han mejorado su calidad de vida y su acceso a la ciudadanía.
Una mirada al presente y al futuro
Aunque el documental reconoce los importantes avances logrados en España, también evidencia los desafíos pendientes. Las dificultades para acceder a información comprensible, al empleo, a la vivienda, al ocio o a los órganos de gobierno de las organizaciones, siguen limitando la participación real de muchas de estas personas y de sus familias.
A través de sus protagonistas, ‘El Poder de las Personas’ defiende una idea sencilla y poderosa: las personas con discapacidad intelectual tienen derecho a tomar decisiones sobre sus propias vidas y a ocupar los espacios de participación y decisión donde se construye la sociedad. Porque, como refleja este video-documental, el poder no debe ser exclusivo de unos pocos: se comparte, se ejerce en comunidad y debe incluir a todas las personas sin excepción.

title: Trivial pursuits build valuable community at Prague's quiz nights
content:
As captain of my high school’s Scholar’s Bowl team, I won no laurels among the cool kids. In a teenage wasteland, it merely confirmed my “geek” status and delayed dating indefinitely. In Prague, however, the credential may finally pay off, thanks to the popular trivia throwdowns that take place almost every night of the week.
While the thrill of victory is nice, the true prize may be the sense of community and opportunity to build a new group of friends.
“The majority of my friends have come through quizzes,” says Dany Hudecek, quizmaster of the weekly Wednesday session at the Globe Bookstore, Thursday session at The Down Under and twice-monthly quizzes at Manifesto Market.
That sentiment is echoed by many participants, including Pete Baumgartner, an expat who has lived in Prague for 20 years and joins two to three quizzes per week.
“There are even cases of people meeting and getting married,” he notes. “I know one couple who met at the Globe quiz and got married. And on one of my teams is a couple that totally met through quizzes.”
“I met my boyfriend through trivia,” adds Barbora Imrišková, a quiz night devotee and English teacher from Bratislava.
Building friendships without smartphones
Having participated in quiz nights at the Globe and James Joyce, I can understand why. There’s a camaraderie forged by teams working together to achieve a common goal. In fact, it’s a big part of the fun.
The banning of smartphones drives bonding, too. Without them, team members must speak directly to each other and work through ideas to find answers. It’s analog conversation at its purest and connects team members more effectively than any digital device, social media platform or app.
“It’s maybe the only place I know where you’re kind of locked in a room with people and not allowed to use your phone,” enthuses Imrišková.
Baumgartner highlights the benefit, too. “It brings you back to 20 years ago, when we didn’t have our phones and had to remember things.”
For Irish-born Luke Ryan, who, along with American Grant Podelco, serves as quizmaster on Monday nights at the James Joyce, the no-phone rule brings some much-needed digital detox, too.
“I very rarely take my phone out for the whole night, and it’s quite nice to be away from it and to just chat with people.”
That helps foster a spirit of inclusion, and it’s visible in the demographics. Trivia nights bring together a motley crew of expats, tourists, travelers and locals of all generations and backgrounds, united in their passion for little-known facts and useless knowledge.

“Can you think of any other place where you’re rewarded for being an unapologetic nerd?” asks Imrišková. “Other people might think your interests are weird and not want to hear about your favorite dinosaur. But here, everybody wants to hear about your favorite dinosaur because there are six of them on the question screen.”
That welcoming attitude rings true for Ryan. “We, and the other teams, go out of our way to make new teams feel welcome and make sure to give them shout-outs,” he emphasizes. “It’s a great way to meet people.”
Solo flyers are welcome, too, and there’s almost always a spot available on a team so you can try out the quiz, as I did. The quizmaster will ask around for you, too, saving you the anxiety of approaching teams personally.
Finding the right Prague quiz night
That said, there is some variation among the quiz communities. Each may skew one way or another in its composition, which might make a difference to nervous newcomers looking to get started.
For example, quiz nights in Žižkov tend to lean younger and more international, especially at places like Philly and Co.’s Original Cheesesteaks and the Clown and Bard, which draw customers from nearby or attached hostels. On the flip side, the James Joyce quiz tends to have an older crowd of long-term expats.
These differences can also affect quiz formats, lengths, team sizes, question types, difficulty levels and prizes. Hudecek will even read the crowd and adjust questions accordingly.
“A lot of the time, I change questions if I see that there are a lot of younger people in the crowd who might not know Alice Cooper, for example. So I can be a little bit flexible and make the quiz a bit more relevant to them.”
That shows how much each trivia night’s personality comes from the quizmaster running it, as each brings their own approach and preferences. Indeed, that’s the biggest distinction Imrišková sees between the quizzes.
“If I go to Mike’s quiz on Sunday at Sally O’Brien’s, I know it’s going to be super fun and kind of modern,” she notes.
Imrišková also champions the quiz nights at Third Coast Pizza and The Cabin, the only two venues with female quizmasters. “For me, as a woman, it’s maybe a little less intimidating.”
Whatever your preferences, Ryan says, “There’s a quiz for every quizzer.”
That said, he does acknowledge the intimidation some may feel when looking to get involved.
“I’ve heard this so many times: ‘I’m afraid to go to a quiz night because I’ll look stupid,’” he reflects. “But afterward, they say, ‘That was actually quite good fun; I got some questions right; no one made me feel stupid, and I learned some stuff.’”
Baumgartner describes this exact experience the first time he attended a quiz at the Globe.
“I just sat at the bar and didn’t play. I was too shy and afraid to participate. I remember Dany asking, ‘Are you sure you don’t want to play?’ and I said, ‘I’m just here watching.’ But when I saw I could answer a lot of questions, I thought it’d be cool.”
Plus, quizmasters want you to get the answers, too, as a blank answer sheet will probably mean an empty chair the next time. That’s why Hudecek pauses each round at question seven to check in with every team and offer hints and nudges to help them along if needed.
This approach helps make the Globe a good option for first-timers, as its quiz is easier and more free-flowing than other sessions. The size of the space also allows for a large number of teams.
Imrišková recommends the quiz at Beckett’s Irish Pub as another good entry point for trivia nights. “Quizmaster Maarten is very friendly,” she explains, “and the questions are a good mix of general knowledge, but also a little bit challenging, which stretches you.”
Regardless of which location, day or quizmaster fits best, the important thing to know is that the door is open and all are welcome.
For Ryan, that’s what keeps the seats filled with many of the same people, even if their team is unlikely to win. “They keep coming back because there’s a good spirit in the room.”
It won me over, too. You can now count me in for weekly quiz nights.

title: Nukus Begins Construction of District for 50,000 Residents
content:
Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Construction has begun on the Yangi Uzbekistan-Nukus City district in the Ashshikol area of Nukus, designed to accommodate 50,000 residents, President of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev said at a meeting on the socio-economic development of Karakalpakstan in Nukus.
Mirziyoyev said high-rise buildings, business, shopping and service centers, as well as green areas, would be built across 270 hectares using modern architectural solutions and energy-efficient technologies. Foreign investors will be attracted to implement investment projects in the new district, he said.
The president also said Mustaqillik Street in Nukus had become a round-the-clock operating zone. After 28 entrepreneurs began operating there and another 50 entrepreneurs expanded their activities, the street's trade turnover doubled within a week.
Mirziyoyev instructed officials to improve the Nur and Elabad mahallas based on the example of the Kichkirik mahalla in Almazar district and create a modern public space in the local park ahead of Navruz.

title: Tinubu: $12m Abuja Entrepreneurship Centre’ll Boost MSME Ecosystem, Create Jobs, Expand Nation’s Economic Scope
content:
Latest Headlines
Tinubu: $12m Abuja Entrepreneurship Centre’ll Boost MSME Ecosystem, Create Jobs, Expand Nation’s Economic Scope
Deji Elumoye in Abuja
President Bola Tinubu has welcomed the construction of the $12 million Abuja Centre for Entrepreneurship, saying the project will strengthen Nigeria’s MSME ecosystem and help more businesses grow, create jobs and expand economic activity.
The centre, funded by the Republic of Korea through the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA), is being developed at the SMEDAN Industrial Development Centre in Idu, Abuja, in partnership with the Federal Government through SMEDAN and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).
Presidential spokesperson, Bayo Onanuga, in a release issued on Wednesday, explained that ACE will support the wider MSME and entrepreneurship ecosystem, providing facilities, technology, training and enterprise support for aspiring entrepreneurs, start-ups and growing businesses, with an initial target of 500 entrepreneurs, 400 start-ups and 1,500 MSMEs.
About $5.9 million will go into construction, while $6.1 million will fund equipment and programmes for entrepreneurs and businesses.
ACE will provide workspaces, digital facilities, training, incubation and enterprise support for entrepreneurs, start-ups and growing businesses.
It will serve businesses in Abuja and surrounding cities, including Kaduna, Jos, Keffi, Lafia, Minna, Makurdi and Lokoja, while contributing to a stronger entrepreneurship and MSME ecosystem across Northern Nigeria.
According to Tinubu, the centre would help in establishing, strengthening and growing businesses.
“Small businesses are an important part of our economy. They employ people, support families and create activity in communities across the country.
“Many entrepreneurs already have the ideas and the determination to succeed. What they often need is better access to facilities, technology, training and the support that can help their businesses grow.
“This centre will provide more of that support and strengthen the ecosystem around them,” the president said.
Tinubu said the Federal Government would continue to expand the conditions that allow small businesses to grow and compete.
“We want more Nigerians to be able to start businesses, grow them and employ others. We also want existing small businesses to have better access to the tools and support they need to become stronger and more productive.That is important for jobs, incomes and the wider economy,” he said.
The president said the project complements the administration’s wider investments in digital skills, entrepreneurship, enterprise development and support for MSMEs.
The centre has also been designed to accommodate women and persons with disabilities. It will include accessible facilities and crèche services for women with young children.
While construction is ongoing, SMEDAN, KOICA and UNDP will work with universities, incubators, financial institutions, private-sector organisations and entrepreneur networks to build a wider support system around the centre and identify businesses that can benefit from its programmes.
Tinubu thanked the Government of the Republic of Korea for the $12 million investment and commended KOICA, UNDP and SMEDAN for bringing the project to the construction stage.
He said Nigeria would continue to welcome investments and partnerships that strengthen local businesses, deepen enterprise development and create more jobs.
“Our economy will be stronger when more Nigerian businesses can start, survive and grow.
“We must keep building the support around them and opening more opportunities for enterprise across the country,” the president said.

title: Federal government urged not to let fire ant eradication funding lapse
content:
States urge federal government to fund next tranche of fire ant eradication
In short:
Advocates are urging the federal government to commit to funding the next step of the National Fire Ant Eradication Program in the next budget.
State and federal agriculture ministers have agreed total eradication of the pests remained "technically feasible, cost beneficial and in the national interest".
What's next?
Funding for the current eradication plan expires in June 2027.
Advocates are urging state and federal treasurers to fund the next step of fire ant eradication efforts, with a funding cliff looming in June next year.
State and federal agriculture ministers met last week to discuss the National Red Imported Fire Ant Eradication Program Response Plan 2027-32.
Queensland Primary Industries Minister Tony Perrett presented the potential impacts and consequences of wider proliferation of fire ants.
Eradication of the pests was deemed to remain "technically feasible, cost beneficial and in the national interest".
Ministers "agreed to consult their respective governments on funding and come back together for a final decision" ahead of next year's budget.
Loading...'Turning of the tide'
Invasive Species Council (ISC) advocacy director Reece Pianta said the program was beginning to see a "turning of the tide" in fighting the spread of fire ants.
"We've seen 208,000 hectares, an area almost the size of the ACT, transition from the suppression zone into active eradication," Mr Pianta said.
"Fire ants removed from the Murray-Darling Basin in northern New South Wales, no new nests detected in central Queensland."
Mr Pianta said if the ants got out of control they would cause more than $2 billion in economic damage each year. ISC modelling suggests the eradication program would cost $1 billion over five years.
He said the track record of funding for the program was "pretty scary", and that the last funding gap in 2023 saw efforts move backwards.
"What that resulted in was about a 40 per cent increase in the fire ant infestation zone. It grew from around 600,000 hectares to about 850,000," he said.
He said another funding gap in the program could see governments lose the chance to eradicate the pests completely.
The ISC urged governments to ensure funding for the next "really crucial" phase of the program.
"There's a responsible program in the field now, the community is backing it," Mr Pianta said.
"We need our governments to fund it to complete its work.
"For our treasurers and finance ministers around the country, the cost-benefit analysis is clearly in favour of paying to complete eradication right now."
Mr Perrett told state parliament in June that fire ants remained "one of Australia's most significant biosecurity threats" as he announced $10.5 million in state funding for suppression efforts in 2026-27.
"Primary producers have strongly supported the suppression efforts because they understand what is at stake … sugarcane, nursery, turf and hay know that fire ants threaten their industries, and more broadly agricultural production, regional economies, and our way of life," he said.
"Noting that a new response plan is being negotiated for the nationally cost-shared program, I again call on the federal government and cost share partners to include fire ant suppression within the next response plan."
Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins has been contacted for comment.
Program aims to strangle spread
Fire ant eradication works by mixing insect growth inhibitor with corn grit, which is then carried to the queen by worker ants.
The bait stunts the growth of the queen, who then cannot produce new worker ants, and the colony collapses.
The biosecurity zone map covers Brisbane, Logan, and Ipswich, and reaches as far north as the Sunshine Coast and south into northern New South Wales, with isolated hotspots across the south-east.
Any materials such as soil or hay being moved from these areas must go through strict biosecurity measures to ensure no fire ants are onboard.
The National Fire Ant Eradication Program targets properties in a broad band known as an "eradication area" around a fire ant "suppression zone", which covers a large corner of south-east Queensland, including Brisbane.
The goal is to treat every property in the eradication area up to six times over a two-year period, before contracting the zone and targeting a new set of properties.
That band is intended to shift gradually toward Brisbane and the coast, strangling the ants' spread.
Properties not within the eradication zone will not be specifically targeted, but residents can contact the Fire Ant Suppression Taskforce and work with them to treat fire ants found on their properties.
Areas are monitored for five years following treatment to ensure fire ants do not return.

title: Gesundheitsinitiative - Kostenloser Kampf gegen Adipositas in St. Pölten
content:
Gesundheitsinitiative in Niederösterreich: Statt noch auf neue Kassentarife zu warten, startet das Ärztezentrum iMed in St. Pölten ein kostenloses, ärztlich begleitetes Abnehmprogramm.
Übergewicht ist längst mehr als eine Frage der Figur – mit den Kilos können auch die gesundheitlichen Risiken wachsen. Das Ärztezentrum iMed in St. Pölten will deshalb früh gegensteuern und bietet ab sofort ein kostenloses Programm zur Adipositastherapie an.
Abgestimmte Begleitung der Patienten
„Die frühzeitige Therapie der Adipositas ist aus verschiedensten Gründen dringend geboten“, sagt Dr. Bernhard Angermayr, einer der Leiter von iMed. Gemeinsam mit seinem Kollegen Dr. Sebastian Klein und Diätologin Johanna Fuchs setzt er auf umfassende Beratung und eine individuell abgestimmte Begleitung. Ziel ist keine kurzfristige Diät, sondern eine nachhaltige Gewichtsreduktion.
Rasche Hilfe für junge Menschen
Besonders junge Menschen sollen erreicht werden – möglichst bevor Folgeerkrankungen auftreten. Bluthochdruck, Diabetes, Fettleber oder orthopädische Beschwerden können mit Adipositas einhergehen und die Lebensqualität beeinträchtigen.
Während die Ärztekammern – wie berichtet – für eine bessere Abgeltung der umfassenden Adipositastherapie im Kassensystem einen eigenen Tarif fordern, wartet iMed nicht auf eine politische Lösung. „Wir warten nicht darauf, sondern wir handeln“, betont Angermayr. Das Programm ist bei iMed kostenlos und wird von den Ärzten und der Diätologin begleitet.

title: Sandbondtenga/Éducation: 57 enseignants de Barsalogho formés au bi-plurilinguisme

Burkina-SANDBONDTENGA-ÉDUCATION-BI-PLURILINGUISME
Sandbondtenga/Éducation: 57 enseignants de Barsalogho formés au bi-plurilinguisme
Barsalogho, 17 sept. 2026 (AIB) – Cinquante-sept enseignants de CP1 et des directeurs d’écoles des deux Circonscriptions d’éducation de base (CEB) de Barsalogho ont reçu jeudi, une formation sur l’enseignement bi- plurilingue. Cette formation de deux semaines s’inscrit dans le cadre du Programme de développement de l’enseignement bilingue et plurilingue (PLN) du ministère de l’Éducation de base et de l’Alphabétisation (MEBA).
Le bi-plurilinguisme consiste en un enseignement concomitant de la langue locale et du français. Le ministère en charge de l’Éducation a procédé à l’implémentation et à l’expérimentation de cette approche avant d’entamer sa généralisation.
Cette formation vise à renforcer les capacités des enseignants à mieux articuler le français avec les langues maternelles des apprenants, principalement le mooré, dans le cadre de l’enseignement bilingue.
Les participants, dont certains sont en recyclage et d’autres en initiation, acquerront les outils nécessaires à la mise en œuvre de cette approche dans leurs classes dès la rentrée pédagogique.
Le chef de la Circonscription d’éducation de base (CCEB) de Barsalogho 1, Jean Marie Ouédraogo, a salué l’adoption de cette réforme, au regard des difficultés rencontrées par certains apprenants dans l’appropriation du français.
« Par sa langue, on apprend facilement, vite et bien. La langue de l’autre nous a torpillés », a-t-il déclaré.

title: World Bank: Poverty in Uzbekistan Falls to 5.8%
content:
Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — The poverty rate in Uzbekistan fell from 17% in 2021 to 5.8% in 2025, with about 3.7 million people moving out of poverty during the period, according to the World Bank’s “Uzbekistan Poverty and Equity Assessment: Towards Shared Prosperity and Opportunity for All,” prepared by its Europe and Central Asia regional department.
The report says poverty reduction in Uzbekistan has been among the fastest recorded in middle-income countries worldwide. Real per capita household consumption grew by an average of 7% annually in 2021–2024, placing Uzbekistan seventh among middle-income countries on this measure. Under the international poverty line for upper-middle-income countries of US$8.3 per day in 2021 purchasing power parity terms, Uzbekistan’s poverty rate declined from 38% to 12.4%. The country accounted for nearly 40% of the overall reduction in the number of poor people in the Europe and Central Asia region during the period.
Similar trends were recorded under other international poverty indicators. At the extreme poverty line of US$3 per day in 2021 purchasing power parity terms, Uzbekistan’s rate fell from 4.4% in 2022 to 2.3% in 2025. Under the World Bank’s multidimensional poverty index, which considers not only income but also access to basic services, the rate declined from 4.4% in 2021 to 2.7% in 2024. The prosperity gap — a measure of how much average incomes would need to increase to reach the level of high-income countries — narrowed from 3.8 in 2021 to 2.4 in 2025.
At the same time, the middle class expanded rapidly. Its share of the population increased from 37% to more than 72% between 2021 and 2025, while the share of vulnerable people — those at risk of falling back below the poverty line — declined from 45.7% to 22.1%. Analysis of panel household survey data for 2019–2024 shows that 44% of the population moved into a higher economic class, while only 11% experienced downward mobility. About one-third of those who were poor in 2019 remained poor in 2024. The upper segment of the middle class in Tashkent more than tripled during the period, although progress was also recorded in other regions and rural areas.
The World Bank noted that poverty in Uzbekistan is no longer predominantly a rural phenomenon. The gap between urban and rural poverty narrowed from 5.9 to 1.2 percentage points as rural poverty declined faster than urban poverty. However, vulnerability indicators remain high in almost all regions, except Tashkent, where at least one-fifth of the population remains at risk. Vulnerability to poverty has a weak correlation with climate risks, which, according to the report’s authors, calls for more targeted and geographically differentiated social support measures.
According to the report, increased employment among poor men was a key driver of poverty reduction. The share of poor men with paid employment increased from 18% to 46% in 2022–2025 amid a decline in labor migration and a shift from agriculture and self-employment toward paid employment within Uzbekistan. Real wages among poorer households increased by 11–12% in both the public and private sectors. At the same time, the report notes that about 60% of poor wage workers are employed without written contracts or basic social protections, while more than 40% work in irregular, temporary or seasonal jobs.
The report also highlights the position of women in the labor market. Women account for 92% of economically inactive adults in poor and vulnerable households, with about 85% citing childcare and household responsibilities as the main reason for not working. Women with children under two are 36% less likely to be employed than women without children. Among employed women, average wages are 35–40% lower than those of men, with the report noting that this gap is about 20 percentage points higher than the global average.
The report also identifies significant regional disparities in economic progress. Despite the narrowing of regional poverty gaps, the expansion of the middle class remains highly uneven and is concentrated primarily in Tashkent and Tashkent Region, which account for more than half of all highly skilled private-sector jobs in the country.
The World Bank’s policy priorities include expanding access for poor and vulnerable groups to quality education and in-demand labor market skills, including STEM and digital competencies; improving transport and digital connectivity between lagging regions and growth centers; expanding affordable, including rental, housing in Tashkent and other major cities to support domestic labor mobility; reducing barriers to women’s employment by expanding access to preschool education and childcare for young children; and improving the targeting of social protection, including by strengthening benefits for low-income families and gradually replacing untargeted energy and utility subsidies with targeted social assistance.
According to the report’s macro-microsimulation estimates, implementing a package of reforms in education and professional skills could reduce poverty by an additional 0.8 percentage points by 2040, lower vulnerability by 2.1 percentage points and increase the middle-class share by 2.9 percentage points compared with a scenario in which current policies remain unchanged.
Measures to expand access to childcare, improve women’s skills and increase the retirement age for women could, according to the World Bank’s estimates, reduce poverty by 0.7 percentage points, lower vulnerability by 1.8 percentage points and increase the middle-class share by 2.4 percentage points over the same period.

title: Social Support in Group Medical Visits for Chronic Pain in Primary Care.
content: Social support is associated with improved outcomes for people with chronic pain and is an important but understudied component of biopsychosocial pain care. We sought to explore how group medical visits facilitate 4 distinct types of social support-emotional, appraisal, informational, and instrumental-among primary care patients with chronic pain. We collected qualitative data within a randomized trial of integrative group medical visits for chronic pain, focusing on 2 cohorts of English-speaking patients randomized to group medical visits. Data came from 16 observed group medical visits, 2 focus groups, and 12 semistructured interviews. The group medical visit intervention entailed 12 weekly sessions combining clinical care, pain education, mindfulness meditation, therapeutic movement, and facilitated discussion. We analyzed data using team-based flexible coding and codebook thematic analysis. The 26 participating patients were predominantly low-income (80.8% had an annual household income of less than $50,000); 50.0% identified as Black or African American, 15.4% as Hispanic or Latine, and 23.1% as White. On average, they had severe pain with a mean intensity rating of 7.7 out of 10. All 4 social support types emerged through structured program components (curriculum, facilitation strategies, program structure) and interactions among peers and facilitators. Emotional support fostered belonging and countered isolation and stigma. Appraisal support normalized struggles and fostered self-compassion. Informational support combined interactive education with peer-to-peer knowledge exchange. Instrumental support provided concrete assistance. Our findings illustrate how group medical visits for chronic pain mobilize 4 interwoven and reinforcing forms of social support as core therapeutic processes. They also highlight group medical visits as a potential model for biopsychosocial chronic pain management among primary care patients.

title: Oktoberfest: Wiesn-Gast bricht sich beim Armdrücken den Arm
content:
Oktoberfest-Auftakt Wiesn-Gast bricht sich beim Armdrücken den Arm
Die Wiesn sind nicht nur zum Spaß haben da – für einen Berliner Gast waren sie offenbar auch ein Anlass zum Kräftemessen. Der 25-Jährige zog beim Armdrücken auf dem Oktoberfest den Kürzeren und brach sich dabei den Arm, wie die Wiesn-Sanitäter der Aicher Ambulanz mitteilten: »Aktuell kümmern wir uns im Akutraum um den armen Kerl.«
Knapp vier Stunden nach dem Anstich auf der Wiesn wurde auch der erste Patient mit Alkoholvergiftung von Sanitätern behandelt. Der 19-jährige Besucher musste den Angaben zufolge gegen 15.45 Uhr mit einer Trage zur Sanitätstation geholt werden.
Wie das Team der Aicher Ambulanz auf dem Oktoberfest berichtete, hat der junge Mann das Wiesnbier deutlich unterschätzt – so sehr, dass er nicht mehr stehfähig gewesen sei: »Seine Freunde alarmierten uns, unser Team kümmerte sich vor Ort mit Vitalkontrolle und einer Infusion.« Der 19-Jährige wurde untersucht und sollte bei Bedarf auch eine Untersuchung in dem Computertomografen bekommen, der seit einigen Jahren eigens auf der Wiesn aufgestellt wird.
Mini-Klinik für die Wiesn
Rund 430 Einsatzkräfte, darunter 36 Ärztinnen und Ärzte, kümmern sich über die 16 Festtage hinweg im Rund-um-die-Uhr-Betrieb um die Gesundheit der Wiesn-Besucher. In der Spitzenbesetzung wie am Eröffnungssamstag sollten ungefähr 140 Menschen auf der Sanitätsstation im Einsatz sein.
Über die Jahre hat sich die Wiesn-Sanitätsstation zu einer Art Mini-Klinik entwickelt. Sie verfügt auch über die Möglichkeit, Blutwerte vor Ort zu testen, Wunden zu nähen und Patienten insbesondere mit Alkoholvergiftungen auch über Nacht zu betreuen. Damit trägt das Aicher-Team zur Entlastung der umliegenden Labore und Kliniken bei.
Auf der Wiesn 2025 behandelte der Sanitätsdienst 7158 Personen. Bei rund 39 Prozent der Fälle handelte es sich um alkoholbedingte Notfälle. Ein gutes Drittel waren chirurgische Verletzungen, internistische und sonstige Beschwerden machten 26 Prozent aus.
Den Frauenfiguren über dem »Teufelsrad« auf dem Oktoberfest wurden Radlerhosen unter den Rock gemalt. Gut so! Wer das prüde findet, hat vermutlich noch nie von »Upskirting« gehört. Die ganze Kolumne lesen Sie hier .

title: Los Gemeliers cuentan cómo gestionaban sus padres el dinero que ganaban de niños: "Con 7 u 8 años nos compramos una casa"
content:
Los Gemeliers cuentan cómo gestionaban sus padres el dinero que ganaban de niños: "Con 7 u 8 años nos compramos una casa"
Basado en hechos observados y verificados directamente por nuestros periodistas o por fuentes informadas.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
La pareja de hermanos asegura que sus padres nunca tuvieron "un interés detrás" de su existosa carrera.
Los Gemeliers llevan desde los cuatro años, cuando aparecieron en Menuda noche de Juan y Medio, en el mundo de la televisión y la música. Por ello, desde el principio han tenido a dos figuras importantes en su carrera, sus padres, "dos personas normales, con trabajos normales", pero que sabían gestionar su dinero.
Así lo declaró la pareja de hermanos en El micro show, pódcast en el que elogiaron enormemente la labor de sus padres, que no solo supieron llevar las finanzas, sino que se adaptaron al boom que vivieron y al fenómeno fan.
"No ha habido un interés detrás", aseguraron Jesús y Daniel Oviedo, en referencia a que lo que ellos ganaban "lo guardaban" para ellos. Y tales fueron las ganancias que antes de terminar Primaria ya eran propietarios (bajo la tutela de sus padres): "Con ese dinero nos compramos una casita cuando teníamos apenas 7 u 8 años. Cuando íbamos a la sierra, decíamos 'papá, nos tenemos que comprar una casita aquí', y nos la compramos".
De hecho, los cantantes afirmaron que, "a nivel económico", apenas han sabido nunca lo que tenían, simplemente le preguntaban a sus padres si podían comprar algo y ellos les decían que sí.
"Me acuerdo de que, cuando llegamos a México, no teníamos ni coche en Madrid y le dijimos: 'Papá, ¿nos podemos comprar un coche a la vuelta?'", rememoraron los Gemeliers, que admitieron que vieron un "cochazo" por la calle y dijeron que querían ese.
A los 14 años, su fama se multiplicó aún más tras aparecer en La Voz Kids y ahí empezaron a vivir —y sufrir— el fenómeno fan, ya que llegaban autobuses llenos de gente a su casa y acampaban en la puerta.
"Tuvimos que vender la casa, de la noche a la mañana. Nos tuvimos que ir a la casa de la playa para ver si podíamos hacer vida normal. Y estuvimos cuatro años sin volver a pisar la casa de la playa porque nuestros propios vecinos decían que era insostenible", reconocieron. "Hemos tenido unos padres que han sabido leer el trasfondo de muchos de nuestros fans, que han sabido llevarlo de la mejor manera posible y no podíamos haber tenido unas personas cerca mejores que ellos".

title: Idarati gets a revamp as govt looks to take the runaround out of paperwork
content:
From looking up an administrative procedure to finding the government service that handles it, Idarati is getting an overhaul as the government tries to move more of the paperwork people deal with online.
The revamped national portal now gives access to 874 online services and lists 2,533 administrative procedures, with the Ministry of Digital Transition and Administrative Reform saying the database will continue to be checked and updated with public bodies.
The change is also meant to address a familiar problem with government portals: knowing what you need to get done does not necessarily mean knowing which procedure or administration to look for.
Read also : Morocco moves to improve digital access for people with disabilities
Idarati is therefore gradually reorganising services around the user’s situation rather than simply listing one procedure after another.
Someone looking for a public service would be guided according to what they need to do, while the Idarati e-Services gateway brings digital services offered by different administrations and public institutions into one place.
The ministry says the portal has been designed for use across devices, allowing procedures to be accessed without a visit to an office where the service is available online.
Search and navigation have been reworked and changes have also been made for people with disabilities.
Users who do run into trouble can submit feedback on the online services they use. The ministry says those responses will be used to identify problems and improve the services concerned.
Read also : CNSS spins off polyclinics, digital operations into two new subsidiaries
An AI marketplace is to offer tools for citizens, businesses and government departments, including systems to help users find services and deal with administrative information. Public-sector employees are also expected to have access to AI tools.
How far that changes an ordinary trip through the bureaucracy will depend on what comes next.
The ministry wants Idarati to eventually make greater use of information already held by the administration. Instead of waiting for someone to search for a procedure, the system could alert them to a deadline, tell them about a benefit they may be entitled to or point them towards the relevant service.
Those functions are not being presented as fully available with the present revamp. The ministry says data and AI will be integrated gradually.
Idarati X.0, the next version envisaged by the government, is expected to go further, bringing digital identity, a national digital wallet and greater exchange of information between administrations into the system.
Under the planned “once-only” system, a document or piece of information already provided to one government body would not have to be repeatedly supplied to others.

title: This Olympic river has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern

This Olympic river has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern

The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.
This weekend more than 600 of the state's most promising teenage rowers are battling it out on the crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River, in the city of Rockhampton.
"We've never had any media wanting to attend before," Anthea O'Loughlin, head of Rowing Queensland, tells the BBC.
But this year is different. In six years' time, the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events in this very stretch of water, which has just passed a technical assessment and been endorsed as safe and fair for athletes.
While sightings of saltwater crocodiles on the river – which number around 500 and can grow to four metres (13ft) long – are not uncommon, state government files going back more than 40 years record no attacks by the reptiles on humans.
And though influential figures at last month's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam made occasional references to "safety", the presence of the reptiles was not their chief concern.
"Fairness" is what's been raised with British Rowing's chief executive Tom Solesbury – a reference to the tidal river's natural bends and currents, which many in the rowing community say make it unsuitable for elite competition.
Drew Ginn, who has won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told the BBC he had concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue.
"Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said.
"I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on."
The German rowing body's president Moritz Petri said athletes had also questioned the sustainability of holding the event some 600km (373 miles) from Brisbane.
But the "so-called impediments" got short shrift from the most senior politician in Queensland, state premier David Crisafulli, who reached for less diplomatic language.
"Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said days after the Amsterdam meeting.
"It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right."
Rowing chiefs contacted by the BBC before Thursday's decision declined to comment directly on Crisafulli's "elites" remarks.
But both Petri and Simon Wickham, chief executive of Rowing New Zealand, said their concerns had nothing to do with regional or urban preference but with competitors getting fair racing.
Petri added it was about what's best for their athletes who will train four years for the event, "dreaming night [after] night of becoming an Olympic champion".
And Ginn said: "If elite means having some expertise in the sport over 20 odd years, I'm proud of that."
Whether it was crocs or currents that tipped the balance, ultimately it was the sport's governing body World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) that had the final say on the river's suitability.
On Thursday they approved it after a technical assessment by an engineering firm and the Games' infrastructure authority – which looked at the riverbed, competition course, river flows, water levels and likely weather conditions during the Games.
"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games," World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland said.
There was also now "confidence" in the river for canoe sprint athletes, said Thomas Konietzko, president of that sport's governing body, Paddle Worldwide.
The state premier was delighted. "The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours," an upbeat Crisafulli told parliament. "It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered."
In backing Rockhampton, the state government ignored a 2025 report it commissioned itself, which found the location unsuitable and concluded the best option would be to use a course built in Sydney for the 2000 Olympics.
The Fitzroy now needs to pass a final assessment of its design, value for money and long-term community legacy. As the decision rests with the state government, it's unlikely to fall at this hurdle.
But a wider debate will continue over whether Rockhampton is the right place to invest heavily in rowing facilities – and whether it can accommodate the 2032 influx of visitors.
The city is surrounded by cattle producers and normally experiences its peak number of guests every three years during Beef Week.
So what about the crocodiles?
They're not mentioned anywhere in the latest update from the IOC and World Rowing and they weren't referenced in the media release about the technical assessment. That report itself has not yet been made public.
The safety management plan for this weekend's school regatta does however mention the word "crocodile" 28 times.
"The Fitzroy River is within recognised crocodile country," it says.
"Event planning must therefore assume that a crocodile sighting is possible… No natural waterway in crocodile country can be guaranteed to be crocodile-free."
Procedures this weekend include suspending racing and competitors returning to the bank if a croc is spotted. The official signal for a sighting is the call of "crocodile, crocodile, crocodile".
Asked specifically about crocodiles, New Zealand's Wickham told the BBC the primary concern was ensuring the "fairest possible course" for rowers. "We would obviously expect any course chosen to be safe for rowers," he added.
The company owned by Australia's richest person Gina Rinehart, Hancock Prospecting, which supported Rockhampton's bid and has pumped tens of millions of dollars into sports including rowing, pointed to "fake media" concerns about risks posed by flooding and crocodiles in the Fitzroy.
"The people of Rocky for many years have sent their own children to train in this river, and for competitions, without a single crocodile incident," a spokesperson said in a statement.
And those who argue the tabloid-friendly crocodile debate is overblown, say the biggest of the creatures live downstream. The less-dangerous freshwater crocodiles are more likely to be spotted in the rowing arena, they say.
Also contested by government is the flood risk, though Rowing Queensland's O'Loughlin says that their schools event was due to be held on the Fitzroy in August 2024, but had to be moved after the course was washed away.
Brisbane 2032's chief executive has said organisers are making contingency plans "as we would for any venue".
The 2000 Olympics venue in Sydney is ready and waiting as a backup – though that would be unconscionable for Queenslanders.
For the school-age rowers at this weekend's regatta, none of this debate really matters as they take to the water.
Among them are potentially some contenders for the 2032 Games.
"For our students, the Fitzroy is first and foremost their home water," says Phillip Moulds, headmaster of The Rockhampton Grammar School.
"The Fitzroy has also been the starting point for many… some of whom have gone on to compete at the highest levels of the sport nationally and internationally."

Koulpélogo/Sport : Les transitaires remportent la 3e édition de la coupe inter métier
Yargatenga, 19 sept. 2026 (AIB) – L’équipe des transitaires a remporté, samedi 19 septembre 2026 à Cinkansé, la 3e édition de la Coupe Inter-Métier du Koulpélogo (CIM/K), en battant aux tirs au but (1-0) l’équipe de l’immatriculation provisoire. Cette compétition a permis de renforcer les liens entre les différents corps de métier autour de la cohésion sociale et de la résilience.
Après deux périodes de 15 minutes soldées par un score nul et vierge, les deux équipes finalistes ont dû se départager lors de la séance des tirs au but. Les transitaires ont finalement pris le dessus, s’adjugeant ainsi le trophée de cette troisième édition.
Lancée le 15 août 2026, la compétition a réuni sept équipes autour du thème : « Brassage entre corps de métier pour une cohésion sociale dans la résilience du Koulpélogo ».
Selon le bilan présenté par le comité d’organisation, 23 matchs ont été disputés sans aucun litige, avec 28 buts inscrits au cours du tournoi.
Présent aux côtés des autorités administratives et militaires, le président de la délégation spéciale (PDS) de Yargatenga, Mahamadou Sarambé, a souhaité la bienvenue aux participants. Il a salué le choix de sa commune pour abriter la compétition et remercié le comité d’organisation, le parrain et les partenaires.
« Le football n’est plus un simple jeu pour maintenir la bonne forme ; il est aussi un facteur de cohésion sociale et de résilience », a-t-il déclaré.
Il a exhorté les finalistes au fair-play et invité la population à contribuer à la clôture du centre médical de Cinkansé.
Au nom du comité d’organisation, le directeur provincial des Sports, de la Jeunesse et de l’Emploi (DPSJE) par intérim, Moustapha Yangané, s’est réjoui du bon déroulement de la compétition, marqué par un fair-play exemplaire et une ambiance fraternelle.
Il a remercié le parrain, Sita Sawadogo, président de Song Taaba FC, ainsi que les Forces de défense et de sécurité, l’équipe sanitaire et les donateurs.
Représentant le parrain, Adama Zampaligré a salué une initiative ayant favorisé les rencontres entre les jeunes et l’animation de Cinkansé. Il a appelé à promouvoir le vivre-ensemble.
Le patron de la cérémonie, le haut-commissaire du Koulpélogo, Saïdou Ouédraogo, a souligné que la CIM/K vise à renforcer les liens entre les travailleurs des secteurs public et privé, au service de la cohésion sociale.
Il a rendu hommage aux FDS et VDP tombés dans la lutte contre l’insécurité, salué la bravoure des forces engagées dans la reconquête du territoire et félicité les équipes participantes.
L’équipe victorieuse repart avec le trophée, un ballon, un jeu de maillots, des médailles et une enveloppe financière de 100 000 francs CFA.

Jorge Palma. Partidos recordam "figura maior" e "voz única" da música contemporânea
Livre, PCP, BE e CDS-PP recordaram hoje o músico Jorge Palma como uma "figura maior" e "voz única" da música contemporânea portuguesa, manifestando pesar pela sua morte aos 76 anos.

Numa publicação na rede social Instagram, o Livre lembrou que Jorge Palma foi "pianista, compositor e intérprete" e "construiu, ao longo de mais de cinco décadas, uma obra singular, livre e profundamente ligada às palavras e às histórias da vida".
"Todos guardamos alguma música dele dentro de nós, e muitas outras nos foram acompanhando ao longo da vida. Embalou-nos na palma da sua mão com um percurso marcado por álbuns que refletiam diferentes vivências e mundos, e por canções que se tornaram parte da memória coletiva de várias gerações", lê-se na publicação.
Recordando-o como "uma figura maior da música portuguesa contemporânea", o Livre endereçou à família e amigos "as mais sentidas condolências".
Já o PCP republicou uma mensagem escrita na página de Instagram da Festa do Avante!, onde o músico atuou, considerando que "Jorge Palma representa de forma insubstituível muito daquilo que é o Avante!: a amizade, o amor, o toque quente da pele no verão, o cobertor de esperança para atravessar o inverno, a vida que temos e a vida que queremos".
Numa nota enviada à imprensa, o BE classificou Palma como "um dos maiores e mais permanentes nomes da música portuguesa" com uma vida e obra que "atravessaram países, juntaram geografias, cruzaram fronteiras".
Com "mais de meio século de canções gravadas no imaginário de várias gerações", o BE salienta que "não é possível desligar a obra de Jorge Palma da sua leitura política e social, gravada em tantos versos de canções que acompanharam debates, conversas e lutas".
"Assim foi também nas posições públicas que assumiu ao longo da vida, contra as guerras, pelo Serviço Nacional de Saúde, pela despenalização da eutanásia, por condições de trabalho e vida digna, sempre pela liberdade", lê-se na mensagem, na qual os bloquistas recordam o apoio do cantor nas legislativas de 2024.

"Uma voz única que deixa uma marca profunda na cultura portuguesa. À família e aos amigos, as nossas mais sentidas condolências", lê-se na publicação.

title: Chesapeake Bay Blue Crab Numbers See Encouraging Bounceback in New Survey
content:
Conservationists working to turn the tide on declining numbers of blue crabs in the Chesapeake Bay, found some good news in their latest field surveys.
After years of worryingly low numbers, the population appears to be responding to some of the measures implemented to build a crustacean comeback.
This year’s field sampling estimated a total population of 349 million blue crabs in the bay—a 46% increase over last year, according to the annual winter dredge survey.
This raised the population overall to the highest it’s been since 2019, says the report from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources and Virginia Institute of Marine Sciences.
The population of juvenile crabs in winter 2025–26 was estimated to be 228 million, which is also the highest since 2019.
The largest estuary in the US, spanning 200 miles from Maryland to Virginia near Washington DC, the Chesapeake supports more than 3,600 plant and animal species—and the crab remains a cornerstone of the region’s heritage and culture.
In the past 30 years, the surface water temperature of the Chesapeake Bay has increased 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit, but our climate craziness—colder in the winter (which crabs don’t like) and hotter in the summer—isn’t the only cause of the crab conundrum. Human industrialization also plays a role.
MORE GOOD NEWS FROM THE BAY:
• Locally Extinct for a Century, Bay Scallops Thriving Again in Virginia’s Chesapeake
• World’s Largest Oyster Restoration Is Big Success – Fulfilling Virginia’s Promise to Chesapeake Bay Rivers
Also a problem, invasive ‘blue catfish’ are hunting and digging up dormant blue crabs year-round, after having been (stupidly) introduced in the 70s for recreational fishing.
Although recreational and commercial fishing was once a major contributor to falling numbers of blue crabs, the catch limit laws from Maryland and Virginia had solved that issue: separate research from the 2026 Chesapeake Bay Blue Crab Assessment and Advisory report showed no overfishing in the bay.
The numbers can go up and down abruptly, due to many factors, but the neighboring states and federal agencies continue to share data and commit resources to ensure a healthy ecosystem.
And their efforts are paying off. Maryland just released a new report confirming the abundance of underwater sea grasses in the Bay and its tidal tributaries in Maryland last year.
A BAY BEAUTY: Scientists Work to Turn the Tide of Oyster and Seagrass Decline in Chesapeake Bay, Often by Hand
Seagrass coverage—critical for the Bay’s health—expanded from 36,799 acres in 2024 to 41,419 acres in 2025, an increase of nearly 13% in a single year. Bay-wide, acreage reached an estimated 89,385 acres – up 7% from 83,252 acres in 2024.

title: Deze sporten zijn het beste voor je botten volgens de wetenschap
content: Bewegen is goed voor je gezondheid, maar welke sport moet je kiezen als je vooral je botten sterk wilt houden? Een grote analyse geeft een verrassend eenvoudig antwoord: stevig wandelen of joggen. Voor de studie werden gegevens van 18.429 mensen van 40 jaar en ouder uit 124 eerdere onderzoeken samengevoegd. Centraal stond de botmineraaldichtheid (BMD), een belangrijke maat voor de sterkte van botten. Dat is vooral relevant bij het ouder worden. Een afnemende botdichtheid hangt samen met zwakkere botten en een groter risico op breuken en osteoporose. Verschillende vormen van beweging werden met elkaar vergeleken, waaronder krachttraining, yoga en wandelen. Ook werd gekeken naar de hoeveelheid beweging via zogenoemde MET-minuten per week, een maat waarin energieverbruik en intensiteit worden meegenomen. Stevig wandelen of joggen leverde de beste resultaten op voor het versterken van de botten. Een combinatie van aerobe training en krachttraining deed het eveneens goed, maar liet op minder plekken in het skelet effect zien. De winst was bescheiden, maar kan groot genoeg zijn om een deel van de botverzwakking tijdens het ouder worden tegen te gaan. Twee tot drie uur wandelen De grens waarbij beweging betekenisvol verschil begon te maken, lag rond 600 MET-minuten per week. Dat komt neer op wekelijks ongeveer twee tot drie uur stevig wandelen of joggen. "We ontdekten dat gestructureerde lichaamsbeweging samenhing met een bescheiden maar klinisch betekenisvolle vermindering van de leeftijdsgebonden afname van de botmineraaldichtheid in de lumbale wervelkolom, het dijbeen en de totale heup.” De effecten verschilden wel tussen groepen. Mensen van middelbare leeftijd en deelnemers met een gezond BMI profiteerden sterker. Bij ouderen en mensen met overgewicht of obesitas waren de effecten kleiner. Stevig wandelen heeft daarbij een praktisch voordeel: er zijn geen sportschool, trainer of speciale vaardigheden voor nodig. Bron: Science Alert

title: A long lost cousin who was dying of cancer found me online and saved my life

Cancer has always been present in my life. It pretty much wiped out most of my father’s side of the family – my grandfather in his 50s, my grandmother in her 70s, one aunt when she was in her 30s and a second one before she turned 60.
So, when my dad was diagnosed in 2015 with pancreatic cancer, I knew, from the outset, that the news was not good. He was a larger-than-life, strong-as-an-ox character and, within a few weeks of diagnosis, was a shadow of himself. He died just eight weeks later and it left us all in a state of utter shock.
I hadn’t really joined up the dots before losing my dad, but it now felt clear that cancer was a disease which was prevalent in the family and we might have an inherited risk. I tried to be proactive. I went to see my GP, who referred me for a series of scans. I was relieved to discover that nothing sinister was lurking beneath the surface.

The four key moments from Burnham’s meeting with Trump
Caroline Wheeler
Political Editor
There was no shortage of trip-wires that could have derailed Andy Burnham’s first meeting with Donald Trump, but in the end, it produced remarkably little friction.
Even without the charm offensive, Trump liked Burnham better than Starmer
In July, when Trump met Sir Keir Starmer at the Nato summit in Turkey after he had announced his resignation, the US President said he wanted to “bring him back” and “make him great again”.
Two months on, that affection has evaporated. Asked about a special relationship that has been up and down, Trump said things were “more up than they were under your last prime minister”.
politics
No Trump attack on UK migration policy
Trump has previously said Britain is “on the edge of disaster” because of “insane” immigration policies, but in New York, he called it “a worldwide situation”.
For a Labour Prime Minister under pressure on small boats, being spared a public rebuke on his first outing is significant.
Trump has previously called the UK “essentially bankrupt” for refusing to fully exploit North Sea oil and for relying on green energy. He has also claimed the country is “dying” under alleged mass migration.
This time he said Britain had “tremendous potential” and compared it favourably with other countries whose leaders he meets but in which he sees little promise.
Many expected Washington to condemn Britain’s sanctions on illegal West Bank settlements.
When asked directly, Trump did not engage. He said he did not know about the move and left the question for Burnham to answer.
It was an odd moment, but a useful one for No 10. A US president who wanted to punish Britain had an open invitation to do so and passed it up.

How the licence fee could be scrapped for a new monthly charge
Adam Sherwin
Arts and Media Correspondent
The licence fee could be axed and replaced by an £11-a-month internet levy – and viewers invited to become “BBC members” – under new proposals.
BBC facing funding crisis
The licence fee is becoming increasingly unsustainable, with 3.7 million households claiming to not need one, while half a million households stopped paying last year, forcing the BBC to find £500m in cuts.
A report from the Social Market Foundation warns the BBC would have to axeCelebrity Traitors if the corporation’s public funding is slashed.
‘Home internet levy’ fairest solution
A “home internet levy” method of funding is most likely to command public consent, the report, commissioned by campaign organisation 38 Degrees, found.
A BBC internet levy would cost £11 per month, an average increase of 35 per cent on the current cost of internet bills, but would be £4 a month cheaper than the current licence fee.
The report also proposed radical changes to make the BBC more accountable to the public by becoming a “mutual-style membership” organisation.
Members would be chosen by lottery to take part in a member council, where they would serve terms of up to three years and be paid for their time.
They would “hold the board of the BBC to account, ensuring that the organisation is meeting its duties to the public”.
Under the proposals, the council would have no control over editorial decisions, hiring talent or decisions on programming.

Royal claims you haven’t heard as Earl Spencer’s book published
With Earl Spencer’s controversial book Swan Song: Diana, My Sister now released, The i Paper has taken a closer look at some of the claims.
Here are five of the most eye-catching.
Charles acted like ‘child’
Then-prince Charles acted like a “petulant” child, according to Spencer. Charles is said to have told the author that he was “lucky” to be inheriting the Althorp Estate while still in his twenties.
According to Spencer, Charles told him: “You’re just so lucky – you know, inheriting when you’re so young. I mean, I’m 43… and I employ 50 people … but my parents insist on treating me like – like a child!”
A closer look at the claims
Spencer claims, via a courtier, that the late Queen Elizabeth II said Charles was “resentful”. “He always resents things. He even resented it when I taught him the alphabet.”
He also wrote about Elizabeth’s apparent response to the news Diana was involved in an accident. “When the Queen had heard the first news of Diana’s being in a traffic accident, she had asked tetchily, ‘What is she up to now?’” he wrote. “This, before the seriousness of it all became clear.”
Diana suspected Charles had ‘tryst’ with Camilla on train
Diana suspected that Charles may have had a “tryst” with Camilla, according to the book. The suspicion followed a press report in 1980 which claimed Charles was seen with a blonde woman on the royal train.

Children as young as 13 have been referred to a specialist clinic with ketamine-induced uropathy (KIU), according to new analysis.
What is ‘ketamine bladder’?
KIU – also known as ketamine bladder – is a painful and severe condition caused by the drug damaging the urinary tubes, kidneys and bladder.
Frequent urination, blood in urine and a loss of bladder control are some of the symptoms.
The UK’s first KIU clinic opened in May 2025 due to a rise in young people with the condition.
Which children are most affected?
The average age of the first 60 patients was 14.
Around 66 per cent of the patients were girls, with a similar proportion living in the most deprived areas.
72 per cent had experienced emotional trauma, with one in five having experienced the care system.
16 of the children had autism or ADHD, or both.
The underlying factors

Research has shown that feeling or expressing thanks can actually alter our brain.

Then, one morning, while working, I got a message from a stranger on LinkedIn who said that she believed we were related and asked for my email address. Naturally, I was suspicious at first, but when further probing revealed that she knew the name of the town I grew up in, I figured she must be legit, so curiosity got the better of me, and I duly gave her my contact details.
She revealed that, due to the public nature of my work and the fact that I had written an article in the past which referenced my small village, she was able to track me down online to let me know she was the daughter of one of my deceased uncles.
She never met her father and was, in her own words, “the product of a one-night stand”; her mother died when she was a child, and she was brought up by relatives in Ireland before she moved to London in her late teens.
She had been recently diagnosed with ovarian cancer and subsequently tested positive for the BRCA1 gene mutation. She was informed by medics that the gene was likely paternal and was advised to let relatives know they may be at risk. And so, she began an online search, which led her to me – a selfless act for someone who was receiving treatment for terminal cancer and had nothing to gain from trying to find a stranger.
We struck up a virtual friendship, and I shared photos of her paternal family – she told me that she cried when she first saw the picture of our grandmother – and I felt the weight of guilt at the enormous fortune I had been bestowed – with grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins on both sides, not to mention the immeasurable gift of having children of my own – while she had none of these things.
She was still living in London, and we made plans to meet, but as I had moved to Ireland and she had a busy schedule of treatment, it wasn’t as easy as just hopping on the Tube. I was determined to make it work, and we had made a loose plan, but tragically, her health deteriorated, and she died before we had the chance to meet – she was just 47 years of age.
Thanks to her intervention, my extended family and I were eligible for free genetic testing, which would determine the presence of a faulty gene. Fortunately, test results revealed that I did not have the mutant BRCA1 gene, but after further testing and an appointment with a genetic specialist, it was deemed that I had a higher risk of developing ovarian cancer and was advised that I should undergo an oophorectomy and (due to a history of uterine cancer on my maternal side) a hysterectomy once menopause had started.
In my mid-40s at the time, I decided that nothing needed to be done for a while – life was too busy, I didn’t have time for menopause symptoms, let alone major surgery. I’m self-employed, with three sons who were living at home at the time and a husband who works long hours. Any thoughts of surgery could wait.
If I’m being honest, I totally compartmentalised the whole thing, because really I didn’t want to do it. I reasoned with myself that it was very unlikely that I would get ovarian cancer, as I didn’t have the faulty gene and what if, by going through the operation, I unwittingly caused more trouble for myself?
What if things went wrong or I was left with lasting side effects? I envisaged issues during the surgery itself and a whole host of varying crises, physical and emotional, which could unfold afterwards.
So, I put it out of my mind. But when menopause started to rear its head during Covid (more joy to add to those strange times), the genetic specialists’ advice crept back into my thoughts. I was about to turn 50 and had three aunts who died before their time – did I want my kids to be telling a similar story because I was too afraid to face up to the challenge?
I had been to see various specialists over the years for check-ups and ovarian scans, but it wasn’t until I was referred to a consultant gynaecological oncologist, who was so insightful, measured and reassuring that I finally felt comfortable enough to agree to surgery. She laid out the facts and told me that if she was in my shoes, she would do the same thing.
She was so open to questions and even when I dithered about the date, told me that I could change my mind at the last minute if I needed to. She was going to be operating on me herself and I really trusted her, so I locked in the date for admission and decided to just get on with it, knowing that I was so fortunate to be able to have the opportunity, unlike my poor long-lost cousin and the various members of my family who were no longer with us.
On the day itself, I made my way to the hospital and, following a pre-op chat where she went through everything again in detail, I gave myself up completely to the expert staff and, following a 30-second chat with the anaesthetist, I was gone and the next thing I knew, I was in recovery.
The surgery lasted around three hours. I was dreading waking up to bad news, but although I was sore, uncomfortable and attached to a plethora of different tubes and devices, I felt fine. The nurses came and went – fixing, adjusting, administering and assuring – as did my surgeon, enquiring as to how I was feeling and letting me know that everything went well.
Having been dreading the moment for so long, it was a case of ‘the anticipation being worse than the execution’, so to speak. I was discharged two days later with a lengthy prescription and a long list of instructions about taking care of myself, which included getting lots of rest, remembering to do physio, going for gentle walks and not lifting anything heavier than a cup of tea.
This all occurred last year and I can honestly say that it was one of the best decisions I have ever made. When I went back for my six-week post-operation check, I told my surgeon that if it wasn’t for the small puncture wounds (which have since disappeared) on my stomach, I would have no idea that she had removed my uterus and ovaries. I had no side effects, either physical or mental, helped by the fact that menopause had already started before my surgery.
Instead, I have eliminated my risk for at least three types of cancer and, hopefully, by taking this action, will be around for a lot longer than some of my family members were. And this is all thanks to the selfless woman, who I never met, who made it her last mission to alert a stranger (me) to the potential risk of developing cancer – allowing me and other family members the luxury of taking pre-emptive and potentially lifesaving measures.
Cancer is something which touches all of us – on average, someone in the UK is diagnosed with cancer at least every 75 seconds – and there can’t be many of us who haven’t lost a loved one to the disease or been diagnosed with it themselves. This is a reminder that early intervention is crucial, and while far from pleasant, it sometimes involves facing the fear and doing it anyway – as the alternative is not worth thinking about.
